newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-JONES LOSES TITLE TO GRIFFIN BY DISQUALIFICATION.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-JONES LOSES TITLE TO GRIFFIN BY DISQUALIFICATION.

text.p: Roy Jones snatched defeat from the jaws of victory Friday, losing his World Boxing Council light heavyweight title to fellow American Montell Griffin by disqualification.

Jones, who took a 34-0 record and a sterling reputation into the fight, appeared about to win by knockout, but Griffin was declared the winner when referee Tony Perez disqualified Jones for hitting the challenger in the head twice while he was down on one knee at 2:27 of the ninth round.
"I didn't want to win it this way. I wanted to win it on a decision," said Griffin, a 6-to-1 underdog who raised his record to 27-0.

The final sequence unfolded after Jones hurt Griffin with a series of blows to the head. Jones was chasing Griffin across the ring to try to finish him off and the challenger backed up to the ropes and sank to one knee, looking to get a respite.
Jones kept coming while the challenger was on his knee and unloaded two solid punched to the head and Griffin keeled over face first onto the canvas.
"I just took one knee to get my head together. I took one knee on purpose, I'm waiting for the referee to start counting and he hit me two times," Griffin said. "It was blatant."
Perez said he had no choice but to disqualify the champion, who was so close to victory.
"He hit Griffin when he was down," Perez said. "He hit him twice, I had to disqualify."
Griffin's trainer, the venerable Eddie Futch, saw the finish the same way from his corner.
"He lost his cool," Futch said of Jones. "(Griffin) got hit not only one time, which could have been called an accident, but then the second had to be deliberate."
Jones complained that the referee should have stepped in much faster and said a lack of a standing eight count made him feel like he had to keep throwing punches.
"When the guy took a knee, he should have been all over me," Jones said of Perez.

"The referee didn't come so I didn't know if (Griffin) was going to come back at me or not, so I bounced back and I hooked him again and the referee still didnt come. I ain't looking at his knees, I'm looking at his face," Jones said.
"I'm just trying to finish the fight. If he comes up off one knee and hits me and knocks me out, the referee's going to count me out.
"I didn't have time to stop and say, 'well let me look and see if he's on his knees.'"
Jones was leading on two of the three judges' scorecards, having scored a knockdown in the seventh round. But for much of the fight, Jones seemed to be frustrated by Griffin's awkward style.
Heading into the ninth round Jones was facing the toughest challenge of his career. According to CompuBox statistics, Griffin had landed a higher percentage of his punches.
But Jones was in complete control and inflicting serious damage when he got carried away and threw the illegal blows.
"I was eager because I wanted a good, exciting knockout," Jones said.
"I fought a good fight, I didn't lose. Nobody beat me yet. Disqualification, I can take that, ain't nobody gonna beat me."
On the undercard, David Reid, the lone Atlanta Olympics boxing gold medalist from the United States, made a successful professional debut.
Reid beat Sam Calderon by unanimous decision in a four-round bout, scoring the only knockdown of the fight with a right to the side of the head midway through the opening round.
